strengths: The dual-phase decomposition is intuitive and practically relevant: Semantic Anchor Disambiguation targets subject confusion in text conditioning, while Dynamic Layout Fusion Attention targets spatial and attribute binding during denoising.

The method is training-free and tested on two substantially different backbones, CogVideoX-2B and VideoCrafter2. Consistent improvements across both provide useful evidence that the idea is not tied to one architecture.

The empirical gains over each underlying backbone are broad and sizable. For example, CogVideoX improves from 0.6775 to 0.7665 on consistent attributes, 0.4848 to 0.6012 on spatial relations, and 0.2568 to 0.3079 on numeracy. Module-wise and alternative-method ablations also support contributions from both SAD and DLFA.

The reported efficiency is attractive: the full method increases measured inference time from 75 to 87 seconds for CogVideoX and from 14 to 17 seconds for VideoCrafter2, which is meaningful compared with training- or iterative-refinement-based alternatives.
The paper is visually clear, well organized, and includes diverse qualitative examples, an LLM layout prompt, implementation hyperparameters, and an honest discussion of dependence on the backbone.
weaknesses: The DLFA formulation contains a potentially fundamental error. Equation 13 multiplies attention logits by a binary mask before softmax; masked logits consequently become zero rather than negative infinity and can still receive substantial probability. The manuscript does not clarify whether the implementation instead uses a proper additive mask, so the central mechanism is not reproducible from the stated method.

Several essential DLFA details are missing: which layers, heads, and timesteps supply the text-video correlations; how correlations are aggregated; how overlapping subject masks are resolved; how layouts are mapped to latent tokens; and how the localized independent-noise strategy is implemented. The VideoCrafter2 adaptation is also only described at a high level.

The claimed temporal schedule for SAD is ambiguous or internally inconsistent. Under the usual reverse-diffusion convention, omega(t)=1-t/T is weakest at the early, high-noise steps, whereas the text states that clearer semantics are needed and emphasized early. The indexing convention is not defined. Moreover, the unnormalized anchor-direction sum scales with the number of subjects, yet robustness to subject count is not studied.

The evaluation lacks uncertainty estimates, repeated stochastic samples, or human evaluation. Reporting one aggregate score per setting is insufficient to establish whether many of the smaller gains are robust, especially for stochastic video generation and perceptual automatic metrics.

The state-of-the-art comparison mixes models with different architectures, resolutions, frame counts, and possibly evaluation-generation protocols, including evolving commercial systems. This makes the broad superiority claim less convincing than the controlled improvements over the two paired backbones.

The qualitative evidence consists of selected frames rather than complete videos or temporal diagnostics. It therefore provides limited support for claims about motion, interaction coherence, trajectory control, and inter-frame consistency. The complex-prompt and trajectory applications are illustrative only and receive no quantitative evaluation.

Calling the approach model-agnostic is stronger than the evidence permits: only two architectures are tested, and both require architecture-specific attention interventions. Dependence on ChatGLM-generated subject extraction and layouts is not ablated, including sensitivity to layout errors or comparison with oracle, random, or manually supplied layouts.

Reproducibility remains inadequate despite listing a few hyperparameters: there is no code or usable project link in the manuscript, no random seeds, no exact benchmark sampling protocol, no per-baseline generation settings, and no complete specification of the attention intervention.

The limitations section is too narrow. It omits failure modes from inaccurate LLM layouts, computational and deployment costs of the auxiliary LLM, possible demographic or representational biases, and misuse risks associated with improved controllable video generation. No substantive research-ethics discussion is provided.

Overall, the idea is promising and the controlled backbone results are encouraging, but underspecified central equations and implementation choices, together with insufficiently rigorous stochastic and temporal evaluation, prevent others from reliably validating or building on the contribution in its current form.

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: improving multi-subject attribute, spatial, motion, and interaction binding in text-to-video generation without retraining the backbone.

The dual-phase design is intuitive: SAD targets semantic interference in text embeddings, while DLFA targets spatial binding during denoising. The manuscript is generally organized clearly and includes equations, diagrams, and supplementary implementation discussion.

The strongest evidence is the controlled backbone comparison: on CogVideoX-2B, the full method improves consistent-attribute, spatial, interaction, and numeracy scores from 0.6775/0.4848/0.7250/0.2568 to 0.7665/0.6012/0.8025/0.3079. Similar, albeit smaller, gains on VideoCrafter2 provide some evidence that the idea transfers between DiT- and U-Net-based systems.

Component ablations show that SAD and DLFA each improve the reported metrics and work additively. The paper also reports inference times, with increases from 75 to 87 seconds for CogVideoX and 14 to 17 seconds for VideoCrafter2.
The limitations section appropriately acknowledges dependence on backbone capabilities and weaknesses on ambiguous prompts and precise temporal control.
weaknesses: Soundness: the central masked-attention equation appears technically incorrect as written. Equation 13 multiplies attention logits by a binary mask before softmax. This sets prohibited logits to zero rather than negative infinity, so prohibited entries can retain substantial probability and may even dominate permitted negative logits. The claimed restricted interaction therefore does not follow from the formulation. If the implementation uses additive masking, the manuscript must specify and analyze that instead.

Soundness: several other core definitions are insufficiently justified. The adaptive mask selects values strictly greater than the kth-largest correlation, generally producing fewer than k pixels and behaving unpredictably under ties; union with the prior mask can expand the area to nearly 2k rather than merely refine its shape. Overlapping subject masks and independently sampled noise in overlapping regions are not addressed.

Soundness: SAD sums unnormalized anchor differences across all other subjects, making its magnitude depend on the number and geometry of subjects without normalization. The mapping from pooled anchor vectors to possibly multi-token subject embeddings is described only as broadcasting. Moreover, under the conventional reverse-diffusion indexing, ω(t)=1−t/T is weakest at the initial high-noise step, apparently contradicting the stated motivation that early denoising requires stronger disambiguation; the timestep convention is not defined.

Evidence: all conclusions rely on point estimates from automated benchmark metrics. The paper reports no number of sampled videos or random seeds per prompt, uncertainty intervals, significance tests, human preference evaluation, or independent assessment of visual quality and temporal consistency. Selected three-frame examples cannot establish video-level coherence and are vulnerable to cherry-picking.

Evidence: the broad state-of-the-art comparison combines scores from models with different resolutions, frame counts, generation procedures, and potentially evaluation implementations. Numerous missing entries further weaken the comparison. The controlled improvements over the two underlying backbones are informative, but they do not justify the stronger claim of comprehensive superiority.

Evidence: the trajectory-control and complex-prompt applications are supported only by a few qualitative examples. There are no trajectory-error measurements, temporal-control benchmarks, user studies, or controlled baselines sufficient to support claims that the method significantly outperforms existing approaches in these settings.

Significance and originality: both semantic-anchor manipulation and region-masked attention are closely related to cited training-free binding and layout-control methods. Combining them for video is potentially useful, but the conceptual advance appears incremental, and comparisons against the closest alternatives are limited to simplistic replacements such as “Word Swap” and one 3D-region-attention variant.

The claim of being model-agnostic is too broad based on only CogVideoX-2B and VideoCrafter2. Both are comparatively limited examples, and their adaptations differ materially; no evidence is provided for current large video transformers or architectures with different text encoders and attention organization.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The project-page field is blank, no code is provided, and important details are missing: exact model checkpoints and software versions, seeds, attention layers modified, token-to-subject extraction, mask resizing across layers, overlap resolution, localized-noise algorithm, LLM decoding settings, metric implementation, and per-category sampling protocol. The cost and latency of ChatGLM-4 layout generation also appear excluded from the efficiency analysis.

Presentation contains overclaims such as “seamlessly,” “without additional cost,” and “consistently surpasses” that are not supported by the experiments. There are also citation inconsistencies and frequent grammatical errors, although the main exposition remains understandable.

The limitations discussion is honest but incomplete: it omits dependence on potentially erroneous LLM-generated layouts, sensitivity to layout and threshold hyperparameters, added external-model cost, overlapping masks, metric limitations, and failure cases. No research-ethics discussion addresses misuse, harmful or biased generation, provenance, or safeguards for synthetic video. These omissions are not necessarily fatal alone, but they compound the evidential and reproducibility weaknesses.

strengths: Soundness: MagicComp shows consistent improvements over CogVideoX-2B across all eight reported compositional metrics; for example, consistent-attribute binding rises from 0.6775 to 0.7665 and spatial reasoning from 0.4848 to 0.6012. Ablations separately support contributions from SAD and DLFA, and gains transfer to the architecturally different VideoCrafter2 backbone.

Originality: The dual-phase decomposition is appealing: SAD addresses cross-subject semantic leakage in text conditioning, while DLFA combines LLM-produced layouts with model-derived attention layouts during denoising. Although the ingredients build on prior embedding and attention-control ideas, their training-free integration for compositional video generation is a useful contribution.

Significance: Improving multi-object binding without retraining is practically valuable. The reported 16–21.4% inference-time increase is moderate relative to optimization- or multi-round-generation approaches, and the trajectory-control example suggests broader utility.

Presentation: The method is intuitively motivated, supported by clear pipeline diagrams, and accompanied by extensive qualitative examples spanning attributes, spatial relations, motion, interactions, and numeracy.

Reproducibility and scope: The supplement provides the ChatGLM layout-generation instruction, sampler settings, resolutions, frame counts, guidance scales, and the point in denoising at which masked attention is applied. The authors also appropriately acknowledge dependence on the pretrained backbone and difficulty with precise temporal control.
weaknesses: Soundness: Equation 13 implements masking by multiplying attention logits by a binary mask before softmax. This does not suppress disallowed interactions: masked logits become zero and can retain substantial softmax probability. An additive negative-infinity mask would be needed. The manuscript should clarify whether the implementation differs from the equation and analyze overlaps where summed masks exceed one; otherwise the central DLFA description is technically incorrect.

Soundness: The time schedule is ambiguous and potentially inconsistent with its motivation. With conventional diffusion indexing, early denoising begins near t=T, yet ω(t)=1−t/T gives zero SAD strength there, despite the text claiming that early stages receive stronger semantic guidance. The timestep convention and actual implementation must be specified.

Evaluation: Results appear to use one generated sample per prompt, with no multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Automated benchmark scores and selected still frames provide limited evidence about perceptual quality and temporal coherence; a blinded human evaluation and video-level temporal analysis would materially strengthen the claims.

Evaluation: Table 1 mixes reported results from systems with different architectures, resolutions, inference budgets, and accessibility. The strongest causal evidence is therefore the comparison with the authors' own CogVideoX baseline, not the broad claim of superiority over all state-of-the-art methods. Comparisons against recent training-free or inference-time methods under a controlled protocol are limited.

Reproducibility: No code or usable project link is supplied, and several consequential details are missing, including random seeds, sample counts, ChatGLM decoding settings, precise subject-token extraction, handling of overlapping layouts, the localized independent-noise algorithm, attention layers modified, and exact software/model versions.

Presentation and scope: Claims of being 'model-agnostic,' achieving 'precise' binding, and trajectory control 'without additional cost' are overstated given evaluation on only two backbones, coarse automated metrics, and measured inference overhead. There are also numerous grammatical issues and citation inconsistencies, such as referring to VideoRepair as reference [28] rather than [24].

Limitations and ethics: The limitations section honestly discusses backbone dependence and temporal-control failures, but omits sensitivity to erroneous or biased LLM-generated layouts and failure cases with crowded, occluded, or overlapping subjects. There is no discussion of foreseeable misuse of more controllable video generation, inherited generative-model biases, or safeguards.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant failure mode in text-to-video generation: simultaneously preserving all requested subjects and satisfying their spatial or interaction relations.

The proposed decomposition is intuitive and useful. SCI modifies subject conditioning, while LAM uses an LLM-planned layout and feedback from the current attention distribution. Equations 1–12 provide a reasonably concrete high-level specification.

The empirical scope is a major strength. Table 1 evaluates four substantially different video backbones, with average T2V-CompBench improvements of 11.70%–29.84%; the method is also evaluated on VBench and, through FLUX, T2I-CompBench.
Comparisons against LVD and ViCo are performed on the same underlying backbones, and Table 5 shows that SCI and LAM each contribute individually and work better together.
The efficiency result is promising: on Wan2.2-A14B, latency increases from 411 to 432 seconds, whereas the reproduced optimization-based alternatives require 686–798 seconds.
The manuscript is generally well organized and visually clear. Its qualitative examples illustrate the intended subject-presence and relational-alignment improvements.
The limitations section appropriately acknowledges dependence on the pretrained backbone; this honest limitation should not itself count against the work.
weaknesses: Soundness is limited by the absence of uncertainty estimates, repeated-seed experiments, significance tests, or even an explicit statement of how many generations were sampled per prompt. Video generation is stochastic, so single aggregate benchmark numbers do not establish whether modest gains, such as those on VBench, are reliable.

The evaluation relies almost entirely on automatic benchmark metrics. There is no blinded human evaluation of subject presence, relational correctness, motion consistency, or overall preference, and the PDF only provides selected video frames. This is especially problematic because LAM directly introduces layouts that may align well with detector-based benchmark metrics without necessarily improving perceptual video quality.

The evidence does not fully support the strong causal interpretation of the “Present-and-Align” decomposition. SCI is evaluated using broad compositional metrics rather than a direct subject-recall measure, while LAM also improves attribute and action scores. The ablations establish usefulness but not that SCI specifically ensures presence and LAM specifically ensures relations.

Several methodological details are underspecified or ambiguous. The paper does not clearly identify all attention layers or heads modified, how layouts are resized across latent resolutions, exact timestep indexing for ω(t), token-span handling, multi-token broadcasting, or all architectural choices for the different backbones. In Equations 8–10, the axes over which max/min are computed and the undefined subscript i are unclear.

SCI's saliency score is a relative softmax classification among isolated subject anchors, not a demonstrated measure of how much original semantics is retained. Its restoration vector also grows with the number of subjects because it sums unnormalized pairwise differences. The paper does not test scaling to many subjects, sensitivity to the temperature, or robustness to semantically similar subjects.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the reported breadth of results. No code or artifact availability is stated; foundation-model inference settings, seeds, baseline hyperparameters described merely as “optimal,” GPT-4o-mini version and decoding parameters, and complete evaluation commands are missing. Reliance on a proprietary, potentially changing API further complicates exact reproduction.

The LLM-layout robustness analysis is not sufficiently rigorous. The size and motion error definitions use ad hoc thresholds, the manual annotation protocol and number of annotators are unspecified, and no inter-annotator agreement is reported. It also does not evaluate subject-parsing errors or complex relations that cannot be represented adequately by boxes and linear interpolation.

Some comparisons combine leaderboard values, reproduced results, commercial systems, and methods with different conditioning assumptions. This is useful context but does not justify all state-of-the-art claims without tighter control of generation settings and layout information.

The limitations discussion is too narrow: it omits dependence on box-representable relations, linear keyframe interpolation, failures from subject parsing or proprietary-LLM changes, scaling with subject count, and benchmark-metric limitations. There is also no discussion of generative-video misuse, bias, privacy, or other research-ethics considerations.

Presentation contains smaller correctness issues, including inconsistent citations for GPT-4o-mini (Appendix D cites reference 18, which is ChatGLM), duplicated references, typographical errors, and incomplete notation. Overall, the idea and results are promising, but the evidential and reproducibility gaps currently outweigh the contribution and require substantial revision before others can reliably validate or build upon it.

strengths: Soundness: The evaluation covers four video backbones and FLUX for image generation. T2V-CompBench gains are substantial and consistent, and the component, IoU-guidance, fixed-interpolation, VBench, and latency ablations provide useful supporting evidence.

Significance and originality: Decomposing compositional generation into subject presence (SCI) and relational alignment (LAM) is intuitive and practically useful. Combining condition-space intervention with layout-aware attention modulation is a worthwhile training-free system contribution, even if the individual mechanisms are incremental.

Presentation: The overall motivation and architecture are understandable, with effective diagrams and a candid—though narrow—limitations paragraph. The review considered the complete manuscript and appendix. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_sample501_han_medium_20260920T175328Z/scratch/7a9a0a6bdbfc40db8a056a72de386cbe/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: Soundness: The central claims that SCI ensures subject presence and LAM ensures relational alignment rest almost entirely on automated benchmark scores. There is no human evaluation, uncertainty estimate, repeated-seed analysis, or direct measurement of subject recall and relation accuracy. Selected three-frame visualizations cannot establish temporal correctness, and statements that improvements are “significant” are unsupported statistically.

The mechanisms are insufficiently validated. The proposed saliency score is assumed to measure contextual suppression without evidence; it can behave poorly for semantically similar subjects, and the restoration vector scales with the number of subjects. LAM thresholds every attention map at its mean and compares it with a box mask, but the manuscript does not establish that this IoU is a calibrated measure of spatial mismatch.

Important mathematical and implementation details are ambiguous: the axes of the max/min operations in Eqs. 8–9 are unspecified; handling of overlapping layouts is absent; and the exact attention layers, heads, token aggregation, mask resolution, normalization, and architecture-specific injection sites are not reported. These choices could materially affect the results.

The GPT-4o-mini planner is a substantial external component and potential confound. There are no oracle-layout, random-layout, planner-free, or alternative-planner controls. The reported layout error analysis uses hand-designed size and motion criteria without annotation protocol or agreement statistics. Moreover, Figure 10’s in-context prompt describes a bear and panda while its displayed layout output names a silver fox and gray wolf, undermining confidence in the provided reproducibility template.

Reproducibility is inadequate: no code or generated layouts are provided; seeds, sampling configurations, exact checkpoints, prompt preprocessing, and many hyperparameters are missing; and baselines are described as using unspecified “optimal” settings. Mixing leaderboard numbers with newly reproduced results further complicates controlled comparison, while a proprietary, version-changing API is required.

Significance and originality: SCI resembles prior embedding/semantic-guidance interventions, while LAM extends established layout-based attention-bias methods. The paper does not sharply isolate what new principle produces the gains. Improvements on VBench are only 0.66–1.26% overall and the T2I gain over HybridLayout is small, yet the prose repeatedly claims strong or definitive validation.

Presentation contains overclaiming and several quality-control issues, including inconsistent citations for GPT-4o-mini, duplicated references, undefined notation, grammatical errors, and the erroneous prompt example. These problems are especially consequential because the missing details affect implementation rather than merely style.

Limitations and ethics are underdeveloped. The limitations section mentions only dependence on the backbone, omitting planner failures, scaling to many or similar subjects, layout rigidity, API dependence, and unfavorable cases. There is also no discussion of misuse, bias, privacy, or deepfake risks associated with strengthening controllable video generation.

strengths: Soundness: The central Present-and-Align decomposition is coherent, and component ablations show that SCI and LAM each improve performance while their combination performs best across the reported compositional dimensions.

Evaluation: Results span four substantially different video-generation backbones, three benchmarks, and an image-generation model. Comp-Attn consistently improves T2V-CompBench scores, including gains of 15.7% on Wan2.1 and 11.7% on Wan2.2, while VBench suggests that general visual quality is preserved.

Significance: The method addresses a practically important weakness of current video generators and adds only about 5% latency on Wan2.2, substantially less than the reproduced inference-time optimization baselines.

Originality: Although the ingredients build on semantic embedding manipulation and layout-guided attention, combining adaptive subject restoration with IoU-feedback attention modulation is a useful and reasonably novel design.

Presentation: The paper is well organized, motivates the two modules clearly, and provides informative architecture diagrams, qualitative comparisons, latency measurements, and analyses of LLM layout errors.

The appendix openly identifies dependence on the foundation model and reports manual examination of all 1,400 planned layouts, including the observed error categories and an effective keyframe-based mitigation. weaknesses: Soundness: The evaluation is almost entirely based on automated benchmark metrics. No human evaluation, repeated-seed analysis, confidence intervals, or significance tests are provided, making it difficult to determine the reliability and perceptual importance of some improvements, especially the small VBench gains.

The attribution of subject presence to conditioning and relations to attention is plausible but asserted too strongly. Attention visualizations and aggregate ablations are supportive rather than causal evidence, and SCI and LAM each improve both categories of metrics.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript does not provide code or sufficiently precise details about layer selection, head handling, token-span matching, generation seeds and settings, or all model-specific hyperparameters. Dependence on a proprietary, versioned GPT-4o-mini API also introduces nondeterminism and future reproducibility concerns.

Comparisons mix reproduced results with leaderboard or previously reported numbers. In particular, the claimed superiority over training-based T2I methods is not established under a clearly controlled common implementation and generation protocol.

The method depends on explicit LLM-generated bounding-box trajectories, so “training-free” understates the external learned component. Evaluation does not isolate performance under incorrect subject extraction, substantially flawed layouts, API failures, or relations that are poorly represented by boxes.

Originality is moderate rather than exceptional: independent subject encoding/interpolation and layout-conditioned attention modulation are close to established compositional-generation techniques; the main contribution is their adaptive combination and video-scale validation.

Presentation has technical ambiguities. The axes used by the max/min operations in Equations 8–10 are unspecified, some indices are inconsistent, and the unnormalized restoration vector in Equation 2 scales with the number of subjects without analysis of stability for larger compositions.

The limitations section is too narrow. It omits dependence on an external API, restricted box-based layouts, possible loss of prompt nuance, scaling to many or overlapping subjects, benchmark-evaluator bias, and generative-video misuse or broader ethical risks.
